title: Death outside Vancouver Island hospital raises questions about rural emergency care access | CBC News
html:
British Columbia

Death outside Vancouver Island hospital raises questions about rural emergency care access

Paramedics responded to patient outside Port Hardy Hospital just minutes after scheduled ER closure

The death of a person outside the Port Hardy Hospital on northern Vancouver Island has renewed concerns about access to emergency care in rural B.C., where staffing shortages have forced some hospitals to close their emergency departments overnight.

The hospital's emergency department has closed daily at 5 p.m. since early 2023 because of staffing shortages, leaving residents of the northern Vancouver Island community without round-the-clock emergency services.

According to B.C. Emergency Health Services (BCEHS), a paramedic at the hospital became aware of a patient needing medical treatment in the parking lot at 5:11 p.m. Thursday, Nov. 19, just minutes after the emergency department's scheduled closing time.

Two additional ambulances responded and paramedics provided emergency treatment before transferring the patient to hospital staff in critical condition.

Island Health confirmed that both its health-care providers and BCEHS paramedics responded and provided emergency interventions.

"We are reviewing the circumstances of this case … and it would be inappropriate to speculate on any factors that may have contributed while that review is underway," Island Health said in a statement.

Officials have not confirmed how long the patient was outside the hospital and what led to the medical emergency.

The welcome sign in Port Hardy, B.C., a community on north Vancouver Island. (Bridgette Watson/CBC )

North Island MLA Anna Kindy, who is also B.C.'s minister of state for rural development, identified the deceased as a woman in a statement on Facebook expressing condolences to her family.

Kindy said she understands emergency staff were available to respond in this case, but acknowledged that it’s “not the case far too often in too many rural communities like Port Hardy that don't have 24/7 emergency care.”

"Minutes matter in a medical emergency, and our government is deeply committed to strengthening those services for people in every part of our province," she wrote.

Long-standing challenges in rural B.C.

Port Hardy, a community of just over 4,000 people near the northern tip of Vancouver Island, has faced reduced emergency department hours since 2023.

When the ER is closed, patients requiring emergency care are transported to Port McNeill — a 45-kilometre drive along a windy highway.

Port Hardy Mayor Pat Corbett-Labatt said staffing shortages had led to repeated emergency department closures at hospitals across the north Island, including in Port Hardy, Port McNeill and Alert Bay.

To address the shortages, she said health officials decided to concentrate overnight emergency services at Port McNeill, which sits between the other two communities, leaving Port Hardy's ER operating from 7 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Corbett-Labatt said the arrangement was supposed to be temporary.

"Myself and my council have been regularly advocating to get our ER back open 24/7," she said.

Paul Adams, executive director of the B.C. Rural Health Network, said similar service disruptions affect hospitals across northern and Interior B.C.

He said improving emergency care will require sustained efforts to attract and retain health-care professionals in smaller communities.

“The ability to staff the facility has become a challenge,” he added. “It’s a challenge to recruit people and retain them in a community that has been underserved for a long period of time.”

He said without improving resources and support systems in rural communities the number of vacancies will continue to grow, particularly in more remote communities.

The province announced a $45-million expansion and upgrade of Port Hardy Hospital earlier this year, including improvements to its emergency department.

The project is expected to be completed in phases by 2029 but the province has not established when the hospital's emergency department might return to 24-hour operations.

Corbett-Labatt welcomed the investment, saying the hospital has not undergone a major upgrade in more than 40 years. The hospital opened in 1980 and handles more than 6,000 emergency department visits annually, according to the province.

The mayor hopes the improvements will make the facility more attractive to health-care professionals considering working and living in Port Hardy.

But despite years of advocacy, she said she has received no indication of when overnight emergency services might return to Port Hardy.

"That's a million-dollar question," Corbett-Labatt said. "I've been asking that question for a long time and I haven't gotten an answer."

With files from Shaurya Kshatri
